questions.prompt: A water utility wants the mean daily use of **all** 48 000 homes it serves. It installs smart meters in 200 homes chosen at random and finds a mean of 412 litres a day. In this study, which is the parameter?
options: The mean daily use of all 48 000 homes, which is unknown
The mean daily use of the 200 metered homes, 412 litres
The number of homes with smart meters, which is 200
The standard deviation of the 200 metered homes' daily use
questions.explanation: The parameter is the population's mean, μ, over all 48 000 homes; nobody has measured it. 412 litres is the sample mean x̄, a statistic that estimates μ. 200 is the sample size n, and the standard deviation of the 200 homes is the statistic s.

questions.prompt: For the same utility, a second random sample of 200 homes gives a mean of 405 litres a day. What does the difference between 412 and 405 show?
options: Sampling variability: each random sample gives a different statistic
The population mean changed between the first and second samples
One of the two samples was taken or calculated with a mistake
The population mean must be exactly halfway, at 408.5 litres
questions.explanation: x̄ is a statistic, so it changes from sample to sample by chance. The population mean μ stays the same, nothing points to a mistake, and neither sample nor their average gives μ exactly.

questions.prompt: Gauge readings on a production line have standard deviation σ = 15 µm. An operator averages n = 25 readings. What is the standard error of the mean, in µm? Give it to one decimal.
questions.explanation: SE = σ/√n = 15/√25 = 15/5 = 3.0 µm. Dividing by n = 25 instead would give 0.6, and not dividing at all would give 15, the spread of single readings.

questions.prompt: The breaking load of a rope has μ = 250 kN and σ = 20 kN. A test lab breaks a random sample of n = 25 ropes. What is the probability that their mean breaking load is **more than 256 kN**? Give it to three decimals or more.
questions.explanation: SE = 20/√25 = 4 kN. z = (256 − 250)/4 = 1.5. P(x̄ > 256) = 1 − Φ(1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668. Using σ instead of the SE would give z = 0.3 and a probability of 0.382, the chance for a single rope.

questions.prompt: A lab averages n = 20 measurements and wants to **halve** the standard error of its mean. How many measurements must it average?
questions.explanation: SE = σ/√n, so halving it needs √n twice as large, which is n four times as large: 4 × 20 = 80. Doubling n to 40 only divides the SE by √2 ≈ 1.41.

questions.prompt: Fill volumes have σ = 5 mL. What is the **smallest** sample size n that makes the standard error of the mean **0.6 mL or less**?
questions.explanation: n = (σ/SE)² = (5/0.6)² = 69.44, rounded up to 70. Check: 5/√70 = 0.598 mL, at most 0.6; 5/√69 = 0.602 mL, just over.

questions.prompt: To save money, an inspection plan is cut from n = 100 to n = 25 parts per lot. What happens to the standard error of the lot's mean?
options: It doubles, because √100 / √25 = 2
It becomes four times larger, because 100 / 25 = 4
It halves, because the sample is smaller
It stays the same, because σ does not change
questions.explanation: SE = σ/√n. With a quarter of the parts, √n is halved (10 to 5), so the SE doubles. The square root is why it doubles rather than growing four times.

questions.prompt:
Times between calls to a help desk are exponential (strongly skewed). The histogram shows 5000 sample means, each of **n = 2** times, with the normal curve of mean μ and standard error σ/√n.
[[figure: st.m6.clt.n2 1]]
Should a normal distribution be used for probabilities about x̄ at this sample size?
options: No: the population is skewed and n = 2 is far too small, so x̄ is still skewed
Yes: the Central Limit Theorem makes x̄ normal for any sample size n
Yes: the mean of the histogram is close to the population mean μ
No: the Central Limit Theorem applies only to a normal population
questions.explanation: The means are still piled up on the left with a long right tail; the normal curve does not fit. For a strongly skewed population the CLT needs n of about 30 or more. The centre is right at every n, but that does not make the shape normal. And the CLT is about non-normal populations: a normal population gives a normal x̄ at any n.

questions.prompt: In which of these can x̄ be treated as approximately normal? The samples are random and independent in all four. Choose every one that applies.
options: Weld strengths known to be normal, sample of n = 6
Repair costs strongly skewed to the right, sample of n = 50
Component lifetimes strongly skewed to the right, sample of n = 6
Tank levels moderately skewed, sample of n = 40
questions.explanation: A normal population gives a normal x̄ at any n, so n = 6 is fine for the welds. A skewed population needs n of about 30 or more: 50 and 40 qualify, but a strongly skewed population with n = 6 does not.

questions.prompt: A machine set correctly cuts parts with μ = 50.00 mm and σ = 0.20 mm. An inspector averages n = 25 parts each hour. At 9:00 the mean is 50.03 mm; at 10:00 it is 50.13 mm. What do the two hours suggest?
options: 9:00 is ordinary sampling variability (z = 0.75); 10:00 suggests the setting has moved (z = 3.25)
Both suggest the setting has moved, because both means are above the 50.00 mm target
Neither suggests a change, because both means are within 0.20 mm (one σ) of target
9:00 suggests the setting has moved (z = 0.75); 10:00 is ordinary variability (z = 3.25)
questions.explanation: SE = 0.20/√25 = 0.04 mm. At 9:00, z = 0.03/0.04 = 0.75: a mean that high happens about 23 % of the time by chance. At 10:00, z = 0.13/0.04 = 3.25: by chance only about 0.06 % of the time, so the setting has probably moved. Comparing the means with σ instead of the standard error hides the shift.
